title: Hand instruments & what they're for
blurb: Examination, restorative, periodontal and surgical hand instruments: recognise each one by its job, and lay out and pass them in order.
question: The dentist has just placed amalgam in a deep occlusal cavity and asks for 'the instrument to pack it down', then 'something to smooth the margins', then 'something to shape the fissures'. Which three instruments do you pass, and in what order?

teach.h: Know an instrument by its job
teach.body: Every hand instrument has three parts: a handle, a shank (often angled so it can reach round the mouth) and a working end, which may be a blade, nib, point or beak. Many are double-ended. The quickest way to learn them is by function: examining, restoring, periodontal work and surgery. If you know what the dentist is about to do, you can predict what they will ask for next and have it ready, which is what good four-handed dentistry looks like.

head: Instrument
Used for
rows: Indirect view, reflects light, retracts cheek and tongue
Feels for caries and checks margins
Carries cotton wool rolls and small items
teach.caption: The mirror is passed first. The BPE probe has a 0.5 mm ball end and a black band from 3.5 to 5.5 mm.
A matrix replaces the missing wall so the filling can be packed against it. A wedge at the gum margin holds it tight so no overhang forms.

teach.h: Placing an amalgam: instruments in order

steps.label: Amalgam carrier
steps.sub: Carries mixed amalgam to the cavity

steps.label: Condenser (plugger)
steps.sub: Packs it down and removes voids

steps.label: Burnisher
steps.sub: Smooths the surface and adapts margins

teach.caption: Many dentists burnish again after carving to smooth the final surface. An excavator removes soft carious dentine before any of this, and a flat plastic instrument places and shapes non-amalgam materials such as composite or glass ionomer.

teach.h: Setting up a matrix band and retainer
items: Select a band of the right height and size for the tooth.
Fit the band into the retainer (for example a Tofflemire).
Place it over the tooth and adapt the band to the contour.
Tighten the retainer so the band is snug.
Insert a wedge interproximally to adapt the band at the gingival margin.

teach.caption: Gracey curettes are area-specific: each one is shaped for particular teeth and surfaces.

head: Instrument
Recognise it by
Job
teach.caption: Molar forceps have a pointed beak that hooks into the bifurcation. Upper molar forceps come as a left and right pair, with the pointed beak on the buccal side.

teach.text: Don't confuse the amalgam trio: the CONDENSER packs it down, the BURNISHER smooths and adapts the margins, the CARVER shapes the anatomy. And a 'flat plastic' is a metal instrument; the name is historical.

teach.body: Lay instruments out in the order they'll be used, usually left to right. Pass and receive in the transfer zone, below the patient's chin and over their chest, never over the face. Pass the handle into the dentist's fingers with the working end pointing towards the tooth being treated, so they don't have to turn it. Keep sharp working ends pointing away from you, and treat used instruments as contaminated sharps until they are cleaned.

items: Examination: mirror (passed first), probe, college tweezers; BPE probe for periodontal screening.
Excavator removes soft caries; flat plastic places and shapes composite or glass ionomer.
Amalgam: carrier, condenser, burnisher, carver, then articulating paper.
Sickle scalers work above the gum; curettes work below it on the root surface.
Upper forceps have beaks in line with the handles; lower forceps have beaks at right angles. Elevators loosen teeth and roots.

summary: You can now group hand instruments by function, name the examination kit, pass the amalgam instruments in the right order, set up a matrix band, tell a scaler from a curette and upper forceps from lower, and lay out and pass instruments safely in the transfer zone.

A.q: The dentist asks for an instrument to compact amalgam firmly into a cavity and remove voids. Which do you pass?
A.why: A condenser (plugger) packs amalgam into the cavity, squeezing out voids and excess mercury.

whyNot.0: A carver shapes the surface anatomy after the amalgam is packed.
whyNot.1: A burnisher smooths the surface and adapts the margins.
whyNot.3: An excavator removes soft carious dentine before the filling.

A.q: Soft carious dentine remains on the floor of a cavity. Which hand instrument is designed to remove it?
A.why: Excavators have small spoon-shaped blades that scoop out soft, decayed dentine.

whyNot.1: A flat plastic places and shapes filling materials; it doesn't cut.
whyNot.2: College tweezers carry small items such as cotton wool rolls.
whyNot.3: A burnisher smooths restorations; it doesn't remove decay.

A.q: Which feature tells you a pair of extraction forceps is designed for lower teeth?
options: The beaks are always pointed at the tips
The handles have a bayonet-shaped bend
They are supplied with a matching elevator
Beaks set at right angles to the handles
A.why: Lower forceps have beaks set at roughly right angles to the handles so the dentist can reach down onto the lower teeth.

whyNot.0: Pointed beaks are found on molar forceps (upper and lower) to engage the bifurcation.
whyNot.1: A bayonet shape is a feature of some upper forceps, used for upper roots and posterior teeth.
whyNot.2: Forceps and elevators are separate instruments chosen independently.

B.q: During amalgam finishing, the dentist asks for an instrument to smooth the surface and improve marginal adaptation before carving. Which is it?
B.why: A burnisher (ball, egg or pear-shaped) smooths the amalgam and rubs it into close contact with the cavity margins.

whyNot.0: A condenser packs the amalgam in; burnishing comes after.
whyNot.2: The carrier only transports the mixed amalgam to the cavity.
whyNot.3: A hatchet is a cutting instrument for enamel, not a finishing one.

B.q: Which instrument is designed mainly for removing calculus below the gum from the root surface?
B.why: Curettes have a rounded toe and half-moon cross-section, so they can work below the gum without damaging soft tissue.

whyNot.0: A sickle scaler's pointed tip suits calculus above the gum.
whyNot.1: A straight probe detects caries and checks margins.
whyNot.3: A mirror gives indirect vision and retracts tissue.

B.q: For a Class II amalgam, what is the correct order for setting up a matrix?
options: Wedge, select band, tighten, fit retainer
Tighten, place retainer, select band, wedge
Fit retainer, wedge, select band, tighten
Select band, retainer, seat, tighten, wedge
B.why: The band is chosen, fitted into the retainer, seated round the tooth and tightened, then wedged at the gingival margin.

whyNot.0: You can't wedge a band before it has been selected and placed.
whyNot.1: Nothing can be tightened before the band is selected and in the retainer.
whyNot.2: The band must be chosen before it can go into the retainer.

C.q: Which instrument is usually passed first when a check-up begins?
C.why: The mirror goes in first to give vision, light and retraction. The probe usually follows.

whyNot.1: The BPE probe is used later, once the periodontal screening starts.
whyNot.2: Tweezers are used as needed for cotton wool rolls, not first.
whyNot.3: An excavator is a restorative instrument, not part of a routine examination.

C.q: Where should instruments be passed between the dental nurse and the dentist?
options: In the transfer zone below the chin
C.why: The transfer zone, below the chin and over the chest, keeps sharp or contaminated instruments away from the patient's eyes and face.

whyNot.0: Passing over the face risks dropping instruments onto the patient's eyes.
whyNot.1: Behind the head is out of the dentist's line of sight and awkward to reach.
whyNot.3: The lap is too far from the mouth and outside the working area.

C.q: A dentist asks for an elevator with a triangular blade to lift a lower molar root. Which do you pass?
C.why: Cryer's elevators have a triangular blade and come as a left and right pair, used to lift out lower molar roots.

whyNot.0: Coupland's elevators have a straight, chisel-shaped blade.
whyNot.1: Warwick James elevators are small, with a fine blade, in left, right and straight versions.
whyNot.2: A luxator has a fine, sharp blade for cutting the periodontal ligament.

reteach.title: Think of a bricklayer's toolkit
reteach.question: If you were filling a hole in a wall with mortar, which tools would you reach for, and in what order?

blocks.body: First you scrape out the crumbly bits (excavator). You carry the mortar over on a hawk (amalgam carrier), then press it hard into the hole so there are no air pockets (condenser). You run a smooth tool over it to seal the edges (burnisher), and finally you trim it to match the bricks around it (carver). If the hole is at a corner, you hold a board against it while you fill (matrix band). Each tool has one job, and they come in the same order every time.

explain.body: The mouth mirror gives indirect vision, reflects light and retracts the cheek or tongue. The probe feels for caries and checks restoration margins. College tweezers carry cotton wool rolls and small items. The BPE (WHO) probe has a 0.5 mm ball end and a black band from 3.5 to 5.5 mm.

explain.h: What the BPE probe's black band shows

test.q: What is the main purpose of the ball end on a BPE probe?
options: To scrape calculus off the tooth
test.why: The 0.5 mm ball helps the dentist feel calculus and the base of the pocket without damaging the tissue, while the black band shows the depth.

whyNot.0: Scalers and curettes remove calculus; the probe only detects it.
whyNot.2: Polishing is done with rotary cups and paste, not the probe.
whyNot.3: A ball-ended applicator carries lining material; the BPE probe is for screening.

explain.body: The excavator removes soft caries. The flat plastic places and shapes materials like composite and glass ionomer. For amalgam: carrier, condenser, burnisher, carver. A matrix band and retainer recreate a missing wall for Class II fillings, held with a wedge.

test.q: After the amalgam has been condensed and burnished, which instrument shapes the occlusal anatomy?
test.why: Carvers (such as a Ward's or Hollenback) shape cusps and fissures into the setting amalgam.

whyNot.1: An excavator removes caries before filling.
whyNot.2: A flat plastic is used mainly for composite and glass ionomer.
whyNot.3: The matrix retainer holds the band; it doesn't shape the surface.

explain.body: Sickle scalers have a pointed tip and triangular cross-section for calculus above the gum. Curettes have a rounded toe and half-moon cross-section for root surface debridement below the gum. Gracey curettes are area-specific.

explain.caption: Calculus above the gum suits a scaler; calculus on the root below the gum needs a curette.

test.q: Why is a curette safer than a sickle scaler for working below the gum?
options: It is made of softer metal
It is used with water spray
test.why: The rounded toe and back of a curette slide along the root and pocket lining without gouging soft tissue, unlike a sickle's sharp point.

whyNot.0: Both are made of hardened steel.
whyNot.2: Hand curettes are used without water spray; ultrasonic scalers use water.
whyNot.3: Handle length isn't what makes it safe below the gum.

explain.body: Forceps grip and remove teeth: upper forceps have beaks in line with the handles, lower forceps have beaks at right angles. Elevators loosen teeth and roots: Coupland's (chisel), Warwick James (small), Cryer's (triangular) and luxators (cut the ligament).

test.q: What is the main job of a luxator?
options: Gripping the crown to rotate the tooth
Holding the cheek out of the way
test.why: A luxator has a fine, sharp blade that slides down the root to sever periodontal ligament fibres and loosen the tooth.

whyNot.0: Gripping the crown is the job of extraction forceps.
whyNot.1: Cheek retractors hold soft tissue back.
whyNot.3: Sutures are placed with a needle holder.
